Chapter 3. The Mystery and Majesty of God’s Nature.
You know, there’s something really reassuring about believing we can understand, measure, and explain everything around us. Most of us like feeling in control—having answers right at our fingertips.
But when it comes to God, that approach just doesn’t work. God isn’t a puzzle to be solved or a problem you can check off your list. By His very nature, He’s beyond what we can wrap our minds around.
Picture this: a little kid standing at the edge of the ocean for the very first time. The waves seem to go on forever, the water’s so deep you can’t see the bottom, and the sound is both soothing and overwhelming at the same time. That child feels tiny… but also unexpectedly safe. There’s this sense that something vast and good is moving all around—something we can’t completely understand, but deep down, we know we can trust.
That’s what it’s like to approach the mystery of God. No matter how much we learn or experience, there’s always more. God is infinite, eternal, and unchanging. He’s not tied down by time or space, and He’s not limited by what we can comprehend.
And honestly, a lot of people don’t realize just how important that is. If God could be fully understood, would He really be worthy of worship? The very things that make Him mysterious are what make Him great.
Now, some folks really struggle with this. They want everything clear and predictable—neat categories, tidy answers, a sense that nothing’s left unresolved. But faith isn’t about having it all figured out.
It’s about trusting a God who’s bigger than any problem, wiser than any plan, and more loving than we can ever imagine.
That kind of trust isn’t easy. It means letting go of our need to control, and embracing the reality that God is both knowable… and unknowable.
I remember a friend who spent years searching for answers. One day, he finally admitted—the questions were never going to stop. The more he learned, the more he realized just how much he didn’t know. At first, that drove him crazy. But with time, it actually set him free.
He discovered that faith wasn’t about having all the answers, but being willing to live with the questions. The mystery of God became a source of comfort, not anxiety.
And that’s when it really clicked—the majesty of God is found in His mystery. The more we try to shrink God down to something manageable, the more we lose sight of just how great He is.
True worship starts with humility… with recognizing that God is beyond our understanding, yet He’s chosen to reveal Himself in ways we can know and love. That’s not a contradiction—it’s a gift.
It means faith is always an adventure. Always a journey into the unknown.
